title: Carlos Alcaraz stops João Fonseca’s Miami party, but Brazilian sensation is in for the long haul
content:
Here’s what the folks who run tennis are hoping.

In three, or five, or seven or 10 years, when Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner are racing to catch Novak Djokovic’s records, João Fonseca and a couple others of his generation will be grabbing their share of titles and claiming spots at the top of the sport.

When they do, the hope goes, everyone will remember March 2026 as when it all began.

First, the night at the BNP Paribas Open at Indian Wells, when Fonseca went toe-to-toe with Sinner in a bashfest to end all bashfests in the desert.

Two tiebreaks, Fonseca with a set point in the first one, and Sinner needing to play close to his very best to prevail.

Second, the night at the Miami Open 10 days later, when Alcaraz’s turn came to take on the teenage wonder from Brazil. One service break per set, Fonseca with plenty of opportunities to steal them back, and Alcaraz’s ability to release pressure with his own serve staving them off.

Fonseca hadn’t faced Sinner or Alcaraz on the ATP Tour before this month. Despite two defeats, in which Sinner and Alcaraz again proved that they recognize big moments better than just about anyone, Fonseca showed plenty to suggest that he can push the two alpha dogs of the men’s game, given time.

“I’m very sure he’s going to do some great things,” Sinner said in a news conference in the Coachella Valley, after Fonseca had spent the better part of two hours crushing forehands even harder than Sinner can before coming up short in a 7-6(6), 7-6(4) defeat.

By the time Fonseca’s Miami date with Alcaraz rolled around, the world No. 1, who relishes the theater of the sport, had already gotten the buzz going. Before his opponent had secured the matchup with his first-round win over Fabián Marozsán, Alcaraz showed up on the tournament grounds in a Brazilian soccer jersey.

“Just before my match, he entered the locker room with the Brazilian shirt,” Fonseca said in a media roundtable.

“I said, ‘wait, good shirt.’”

Then came Friday at Hard Rock Stadium, Brazilian fans lining the stands and cheering Fonseca to the rafters. No place Alcaraz would rather be, even with plenty more of those soccer jerseys in the seats. More than 300,000 Brazilians live in South Florida, making it one of the largest concentrations of Brazilians outside of Brazil.

Very early in a 6-4, 6-4 win, Alcaraz, clad in orange, the official color of the tournament, made it clear he was the king in the building.

On a break point at 1-1, Fonseca banged a serve out wide. Alcaraz reared back and ripped a 95 mph forehand across the court for a winner, then skipped his way to the bench.

He likes to win. He really likes winning by beating an opponent at their own game.

Then off they went, on a journey of can-you-top-this shotmaking and power-ball under the roars echoing around the big football stadium north of Miami. Two games later, Alcaraz had Fonseca on the ropes again. But now it was Fonseca’s turn. He ripped a 104 mph forehand across and past Alcaraz. Another Fonseca blast a couple of points later got him the game and kept him just one service break behind, but Alcaraz dismissed every opportunity he created.

Against Sinner, on slower courts at Indian Wells, Fonseca’s movement was less exposed. On quicker courts, against Alcaraz’s variety, he found himself maneuvered out of points more often.

Fonseca, 19, was a sensation early last year, blasting No. 9 seed Andrey Rublev off the court on his Grand Slam debut at the 2025 Australian Open before winning his first ATP Tour title at the Argentina Open in Buenos Aires.

Spring and summer were tougher, before Fonseca found his way in the fall, when he won the Swiss Indoors Basel in his penultimate tournament of the season. At the start of 2026, Fonseca, managing a chronic back injury, endured a few more tough losses.

Fonseca, with his howitzer groundstrokes, potent serve and developing feel is less primed to upset top players now than some of his contemporaries.
Learner Tien, 20, has six top-10 wins to one for Fonseca, as well as leading him in the rankings, though Fonseca has won all three of their tour-level meetings. Jakub Mensík, also 20, has won the biggest title of the three, at last year’s ATP Masters 1000 Miami Open. Fonseca’s potential ceiling, what could happen when he harnesses all that power and learns when to deploy it, promises so much.

Fonseca ended his full debut year on the main tour as world No. 25, higher than Alcaraz, Sinner, Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer, his idol, managed in their first full seasons at the top level.

Now the head-to-heads are coming around, and Sinner and Alcaraz are ready for them. Fonseca, meanwhile, has showed enough signs the past 10 days that he is going to be.

He had a break point in the first set against Alcaraz and should have had more. Alcaraz was down 0-30 twice.

In the second, Alcaraz powered his way to a break in the first game, but he needed a big serve and a massive swinging forehand volley to save a break point in the second. Fonseca, who had been philosophical heading into the match, kept swinging.

“Facing Alcaraz is just a great experience for me,” he said in a news conference after his first round win.

“For me, as a teenager in the second year on tour, facing those guys is just important for my development, at any time.

“I wanted to face them, to see how I am, my level, where I can go, what those guys do that the other players don’t, how they deal with pressure.”

After the match with Sinner, he had gone to sleep thinking he had faced the No. 2 player in the world and taken him to the edge. He’d had opportunities, and had not taken them. He’d played well, but as he lay in bed he was already thinking about what he could have done better.

Even though he was again a heavy underdog against Alcaraz, he needed to walk onto the court thinking he could win.

“If not, I’m just not gonna have any chance,” he said.

Two great matches, win or lose, do not make a season or launch a career. Consistency, quality and even greatness do. That’s what Sinner and Alcaraz produce.

“They can play in a high, high level for a long period, and they don’t usually have weakness,” Fonseca said. “You need to serve well, you need to do everything almost perfect to win.”

Perfection, of course, is impossible in a sport where the best players lose nearly half the points they play. For now he just wants to get in the same zip code of to where Sinner and Alcaraz are. He’s not there yet, but he looks to be on his way.
